gap: B, near-field asset and material fidelity. Check: in the bottom ~40% of the frame, no object may read as blockout. The sign base and median kerb need bevelled edges, a concrete or painted-metal response, grime and edge wear. The median plants need to be dense, multi-layered foliage with translucency and self-shadowing, with no blocky clumps. The asphalt needs fine aggregate grain at sharp texel density and coherent wear (tyre-track polish, crack and patch seams, faded paint), with no blotchy high-contrast mottling or visible tiling.

Judge: The commercial game frames won all four pairs clearly, and none of the pairs was close to indistinguishable. Its frames are staged marketing shots with a hero subject, so they have a composition advantage over the in-development game's HUD gameplay cameras. Even after discounting that, and the HUD and logo overlays, the in-development game loses on materials, density and believability. It has real strengths: an attractive backlit sky and haze, a recognisable Singapore-like identity (shophouses, rain-tree avenues, landmark skyline) and warm sun. Its failures repeat across frames. (1) The same blotchy, mottled asphalt with no aggregate grain or wear logic appears in pairs 1, 2 and 4, and it dominates the foreground. (2) Median planters of blocky low-poly plants appear in pairs 1, 2 and 4; in pair 2 they also intrude into the chase camera. (3) Placeholder or blockout elements show up as the sign on a beige box plinth, the bare-dirt lots along a 'city street', identical tiled-window towers and a lone hangar box. (4) Streets are empty of traffic and pedestrians, and the aerial view reads as a toy diorama. In priority order, the fixes are: rebuild the asphalt material, replace the median foliage, replace every dirt lot with built frontage, then populate the streets and roofs. Only the helicopter frame (pair 3 B) genuinely impressed. The yellow-car shot (pair 2 B) also gets a wow, because its backlit cinematic lighting and paint work stand out, despite the heavy flare. The other commercial shots are polished but last-gen in texture fidelity, and no in-development frame impresses.
